I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether or not certain documents might be laid on the table of the house with respect to the convention between the United Kingdom and the United States of America in regard to the regulation of the liquor traffic, which convention was signed at Washington on January 23, 1924, and ratified on May 22 of that year. speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a very
few moments at my disposal, so the house will pardon me if I go hurriedly. When the house rose last night I was discussing the reasonableness of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in coming to the conclusion that Mr. Whittaker had been re-established, and I said that Whether or not Mr. Whittaker's business prospects were as he said in his affidavit, in which

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Ralston
he stated that he would probably have to sell at a loss, or whether they were as he stated in the newspaper, in which he said he expected to go on successfully, it seemed to me there was ample evidence by which a reasonable man could come to the conclusion that Mr. Whittaker had been re-established.
I want to make just one point in this connection. There is an idea abroad throughout the country, due to regulations regarding long service pensions, that a man's salary is affected in some way by his pension. That is so in certain cases with regard to long service pensions, but I want hon. gentlemen to understand that disability pensions do not affect a man's salary in the public service in any way. That is to say, Mr. Whittaker could be enjoying the position which he held for five years with the soldier settlement board; he could be enjoying his position as book-keeper and office manager with the St. Williams Preservers, Limited; he could carry on his own business and his revenue would be in no way affected by his pensioner his pension by his revenue.
I would like to point out one matter which I think has been omitted from the record. The other evening the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in reading the notice of appointment which was sent to Mr. Whittaker and which appears in Hansard at page 1672, only read down to the signature of the secretary. I feel sure that he must have intended to go on, but his attention was apparently distracted and as a result the certificate does not appear in the record complete. I have only a moment or two left, but I think it is important that that certificate be completed. The balance of the certificate which the hon. leader of the opposition read into Hansard at page 1672, is as follows:
Civil Service Act, 1918: Sec. 13. (1) The deputy head may at any time before the expiration of six months reject any person assigned or appointed to a.ny position under his control or direction, or he may extend the period of probation within which such person may be rejected for another six months; and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation, shall be reported by the deputy head to the commission.
(2)	Where a person is rejected the commission shall thereupon select another person to take the place of the one rejected.
(3)	The commission shall, after investigation, decide whether the name of a rejected person shall be struck off the list as unfit for the service generally or whether he shall be allowed a trial in some other position for which he may be eligible.
(Ruling of the Department of Justice dated the 9th December, 1919: "If the deputy be reasonably satisfied upon preliminary examination of the person nominated that the latter is
unsuitable or not qualified for the duties of the office or employment to w-hich he is assigned, I think he may, if he think it advisable, reject him without entrusting him with the discharge of any duties; otherwise in conceivable cases considerable prejudice to the public service might ensue.")
Then follow sections 14 and 31 of the act regarding oaths to be taken by officials.
The last paragraph which was read by the hon. leader of the opposition directed the attention of Mr. Whittaker to the ruling of the Department of Justice, and Mr. Whittaker therefore knew when he received that so-called notice, which after all is not a notice of appointment, but a certificate of selection subject to the physical fitness of the applicant, that he was not entitled as of right to probation under the ruling of the Department of Justice.
I would like to say a further word with regard to probation. It seems almost unreasonable to talk about taking a man on probation who has been reported on by the responsible officers of the department, not once, but twice, and not by one officer, but by three, and solemnly putting him on probation for one, two, three, or six months. What would happen? Mr. Collver, who has only a seventy-five per cent disability, and who had been reported on as physically unfit, would want to be put on probation next, and so on down the line. We have the minister taking the position, which seems to be fair I believe in the opinion of members of this house, that those are the reports the commission has asked for, those are the reports which came to him, and on those reports he made his decision.
Our friends have talked a good deal with regard to the fact that Mr. Whittaker was a-one hundred per cent disability case. As I said last night, we all realize his disability and have every sympathy with him as a disabled veteran with a fine war record, but let us not forget the fact that the difficulty with regard to ex-service men is not confined to one hundred per cent disability cases. Sometimes I find even more difficulty; I believe other hon. members of the house find more difficulty, and the Department of Pensions often finds a great deal more difficulty in endeavouring to re-establish men with 30, 40, and 50 per cent disability. These men are receiving only a portion of the full pension and they have difficulty in finding jobs where their limited capacity can be utilized and thus enable them to make up their income to a living standard. We must remember that while this is a one hundred per cent disability case, at the same time there are other

cases of disabilities, perhaps not so great but in connection with which the men have almost as great a handicap in the labour market as men with one hundred per cent disability and who are receiving one hundred per cent pension.
Time.

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing to-day, as we have on one or two previous occasions, an amendment to the motion to go into supply. That amendment is as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this house the Postmaster General has acted in a most arbitrary manner and in utter disregard of the letter and the spirit of the Civil Service Act in connection with the recent appointment of a postmaster at the town of Simcoe."
I wish to draw particular attention to the words in the resolution " in utter disregard of the letter and the spirit of the Civil Service Act." The terms of the act have been discussed at considerable length, but the only attempted defence has been that which was made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) last evening, and during the few minutes remaining to him this afternoon. The action of the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) has identified the government with the Postmaster General in regard to this particular case and in regard to the other cases which have been brought forward as illustrations in support of our argument and in support of this amendment.
Let me refer first to the Minister of Public Works. Last night he referred to the action of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in this regard as being exemplary. He said it was the action of the best postmaster general which Canada had ever had. He also stated that the opposition had no right to bring this matter forward because the two individuals .who were more particularly concerned were Liberals. Because Mr. Bowyer and Mr. Whittaker were Liberals the Minister of Public V orks asked what right the Conservative opposition had to bring the matter forward. I will answer the minister very definitely. The right we have of bringing this matter forward is the right of every citizen of Canada to have his grievances aired in parliament; that is the right. That is a right which we propose to use on behalf of any citizen whose case appeals to us as being a fair and proper one to bring to parliament. Rarely has there been a case which has been more clearly Within that right than the particular case now 
before us, where the government itself, through the action of one of its responsible ministers, has over-ridden and derided the Civil Service Act.
My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence intimated that the Postmaster General had no other course open to him. As I proceed this afternoon I trust that I shall be able to show that there was a different course, not only open to the Postmaster General, but obligatory upon him to follow.
There are three parties to this dispute. In the first place, there is the public; in the second place, there is the civil service of Canada; and in the third place, there is the Postmaster General. Mr. Whittaker is the victim in the case, but the parties to the dispute are the three whom I have mentioned.
In regard to the public, there is the right of citizens of Canada to apply for admission to the civil service of Canada. They have a further right; if they comply with the provisions of the Civil Service Act, they have the right to expect, if they are successful under that act, that they shall receive as a reward for their application whatever position may be vacant. There is another right the public has. It is clearly set down in the statute that certain forms of examinations shall be followed, and a decision shall be arrived at as a result of those examinations. The public has still another right; they are the taxpayers of Canada and they have the right to demand that the government of Canada and its ministry shall follow the act in letter and spirit, as we say in our amendment. I pause here to say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that unless the government, whether it is this government or any other government, enters into the administration of the Civil Service Act in spirit as well as in letter, then there can be no successful administration of that act. If a minister, or the government itself, is to be permitted to evade that act by a strict or a strained interpretation of the letter of the law, or by a disregard of the spirit of the law, then there is no hope for the successful administration of that act.
If this house by rejecting this resolution approves of the stand of the Postmaster General, as the government is asking the house to do; if this house does that and approves of the actions of the Postmaster General in this case *and in scores of other cases of which this is but an illustration, then I say that you are undermining the confidence of the people of Canada in the civil service and you are disorganizing the civil service itself. You are reducing the efficiency of the service and you are interfering with discipline and coordination

Simcoe Post mastership-Mr. Stevens
within the service. What hope is there for the civil servants of Canada if this act is ignored, this act which is their charter of liberty, shall I say?-under which they expect, when they claim rights, their rights will be respected?
As regards the government, I have already intimated that the government has identified itself in this matter with the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot); it is behind him and, through the mouth of its spokesman iput up last night, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott), it has declared that he is, in this action and in his record with regard to these matters that we have brought forward during the last few days, the best Postmaster General that Canada has ever had.
Hear, hear!

We now have not only
the government but the whole party behind the Postmaster General. What are the facts in this case? The}' are clear and comparatively simple. In the first place, there is a post office vacancy; second, there are twenty-two applications to fill the vacancy under the terms of the Civil Service Act. Let me pause at this moment to bring to the attention of the house what the Civil Service Act states, because this is not some regulation that may be passed at the will or the whim of a government. It would be well for the house to realize that this is a statute of Canada, brought into being by, I think, the united opinion of the parliament of Canada, as a necessity in this day. It is a departure from what obtained twenty, thirty years ago. The minister has repeatedly stated, and in fact his sole defence is that years ago, in 1896, 1905. 1911, 1912 and so forth, Conservatives or others have done as he has done in this instance. But the Civil Service Act was passed in 1918 for the purpose of doing away with the very abuses which, he states, were practised by Conservatives, Liberals and others in years gone by. The Civil Service Act is the product of parliament in response to a nation-wide demand for a departure from the old spoils system and for the erecting in this country of some orderly method of dealing with the great civil service. It is quite clear to anyone that twenty, thirty, or forty years ago the civil service of Canada, in its scattered condition as it was then, was a comparatively small affair. When I went into the west thirty-five years ago there were comparatively few people and the settlements on the prairies were few and far between, with very little of the civil service organization in that vast
west. What is the situation to-day? There are several million people, great cities, well organized communities, immense public business, hundreds of millions of dollars being collected here and there and passed on to the treasury of Canada. Under what?-a civil service who now come under the act, and the necessity for the act has been demonstrated beyond all peradventure. So we have twenty-two people making application under the act. What does the act say? It says:
Save as otherwise provided in this act or in any regulation made hereunder, neither the governor in council nor any minister, officer of the crown board or commission, shall have power to appoint or promote any employee to a position in the civil service.

What section is
that?

Simcoe Postmaslership-Mr. Stevens
only two, because it is not necessary for the moment to deal with the others. One was Mr. Whittaker and the other was Mr. Bowyer. In the first place, Mr. Bowyer was disqualified under section 21, not being a resident of the district. In the second place, he was without question re-established. Mr. Whittaker, on the other hand, was a double amputation case in receipt of 100 per cent pension, but a resident of the district and reported by the officials to be competent for the position. It is true that over a period, a hiatus of six months, where there was a long delay in making the final selection, due entirely-and this is significant-to negligence or delay on the part of officials of the Post Office Department to make their report, some question arose whether Mr. Whittaker could physically carry on the job. After the Civil Service Commission under the terms of the act received the reports of the inspector of the Post Office Department, they gave a certificate which was read by the minister a moment ago and which, I think he said, was a certificate of application. As a matter of fact, the certificate is one of appointment of postmaster. Those words are in large leaded type at the head of the notice.

It is a certificate of
selection.

My hon. friend says it is a certificate of selection. I am going to read the certificate itself. It is headed:
Civil Service Commission of Canada
Certificate of appointment of postmaster.
I would ask my hon. friend to read the certificate.

This was one of the last points of defence of the Postmaster General. He said that it was not an appointment; that it was just an intimation that the man was selected. Not only was it an appointment, but it was so accepted by Mr. Whittaker. According to the file Mr. Whittaker sold out his business. But this is not the only case.
What does the paper itself say? That is the point.
I shall have a lot to say about this paper, I may tell the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), before I am through.
Read it.

I will read it, certainly, and if my hon. friend is very anxious I will deal with that part now, although I had intended to take it up later. It says:
Certificate of Appointment of Postmaster
As the Solicitor General apparently wants all the hieroglyphics, I will give them too:

Dispense.

Now I come to the point that my hon. friends opposite want to inveigle me into reading, and which I am going to read and deal with. The minister has just said within the last twenty minutes that this man was rejected because he was re-established.
No.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said a moment ago that this man was rejected because he was re-established.
No.
I cannot contradict the minister, but invite him to read Hansard and see if I am not correct.
I invite my hon. friend to read it too.

On the certificate is printed this note:
Appointment subject to physical fitness.
Ah!

My hon. friend in the back seat says, "Ah!" Now what does that qualification mean? It means this: Mr. Whittaker was a double amputation case. Much has been made of that fact. The Postmaster General says that this man could not properly handle the position because he had to handle large sacks of mail; that was the argu-

ment of the Postmaster General. Now m this post office we find that there are five clerks. The Postmaster General says that Whittaker was rejected because he was physically unfitted to handle heavy bags of mail. Here is a post office with five clerks, and the chief occupation of the postmaster, according to the Postmaster General, is to handle heavy bags of mail. The thing is absurd.

May I correct my hon. friend, who, I am sure, does not wish to state anything that is wrong? I did not say that Whittaker was rejected because of that fact.
I said that he was rejected because of the report of the inspector which stated that fact.

We have a new reason for his rejection almost every moment. Eveiy time you knock down one argument, another is raised. I say that the Postmaster General has repeatedly stated during the last few days that this man could not handle heavy sacks of mail, and I leave that to the judgment of the house. What are the facts? Mr. Whittaker was found to be qualified in every way, but during that hiatus of six months of which I spoke, the query was insinuated, not in the Civil Service Commission, but in the Post Office Department that possibly Whittaker was not physically fit, and so the Civil Service Commission-the body constitutionally authorized to decide

I invite the Prime Minister to remember-say, after studying all the reports that Whittaker was fit for the position, that his physical fitness was a question which might possibly be demonstrated under section 24.
Now we come to section 24, and I come to the Minister of National Defence. But first I will take the Postmaster General. The other day he stated in his place-I have the Hansard here, but I shall not trouble reading it-that my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart) had attempted to mislead the house because he did not read all the file, and then the Postmaster General produced a little scribbled piece of paper which I have here, and read from that what he said was the opinion of the Justice department. and so on. The Postmaster General said: This is the opinion of a Tory Minister of justice, given to a Tory government, and he left the impression on the house that the

a barrister at law, of ability and wide experience.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends who say, " Hear, hear," cannot applaud that statement too highly so far as my opinion of the minister is concerned. I want to put to him this, and the very excellence of his standing, thus evidenced by his colleagues, will add weight

to what his answer must be. Supposing he is practising before the courts of any province in this country. He is pleading a case, and in his argument before the court he cites a judgment that had previously been handed down by another court, and in citing that judgment he reads one or two clauses which give to the court a certain viewpoint of that judgment from which he was quoting that was contrary to the whole judgment. If the deputy be reasonably satisfied upon preliminary examination of the person nominated-

On April 19 the Postmaster General read a statement which he said had been prepared by the department in reference to the complaint I made with respect to the appointment of a stenographer, grade 2, in the New Westminster post office. This statement appears in Hansard at pages 1727 and 1728. but it does not seem to be very accurate. Some mistakes appear which

Supply-Post Office
may be due to copying and some misstatements of fact are apparent, which no doubt occurred inadvertently. The first line of this statement is as follows:
When Miss K. T. Mawson, the postmistress, requested that a nnale stenographer be appointed-
Something is wrong there; Miss K. T. Maw-son was not postmistress at New Westminster; a postmaster was in charge of that office. Later in the same statement I find the following paragraph:
Subject to Miss K. T. Mawson's resignation in July, 1928-
As a matter of fact Miss Mawson did not resign in 1928, but on July 23, 1925. That is shown by a letter in the file dated November 20, 1925, signed by the postmaster at New Westminster. This is rather important because of certain events which occurred after Miss Mawson's resignation. If we have the right date, namely, July 23, 1925, instead of July, 1928, it makes considerable difference. I think the minister will accept the statement that the resignation was made in July, 1925, instead of July, 1928.
While it is quite true that the Postmaster at New Westminster suggested in 1925 that it would be better to have a male stenographer in his office, his suggestion was questioned by the chief superintendent of post office services. In a letter from the superintendent to the postmaster, dated November 13, 1925, the following statement appears:
However, it is of the opinion-
That is, the department is of the opinion -that suitable work can be found in an office the size of Neav Westminster which a female stenographer could suitably perform in the time not occupied in stenographic duties. This is the action that is being taken in other offices of the same grade as New Westminster when the postal clerk position requiring a knowledge of stenographic work becomes vacant, and it is found to be working out satisfactorily.
The minister makes another allegation that the request for the appointment of a stenographer at New Westminster was for a male stenographer. I refer to a letter dated June 27, 1928, from the postmaster at New Westminster to the chief superintendent of post office service at Ottawa, and which reads as follows:
Authority having been given for the promotion of Mr. Harold G. Wade, at present employed as stenographer grade 2 in the New Westminster post office, to the position of postal clerk, I would ask that authority be given for the employment of a stenographer in his place.
That is not for a male stenographer at all, but simply for a stenographer. I find also 78594-1174
that the advertisement which was issued by the Civil Service Commission in connection with this matter called for a stenographer and not for a male stenographer.
I think the Postmaster General endeavoured to give the impression that there was not very much in this case, that no one could have any real complaint. In that connection I would point out that there are some thirteen ladies in my constituency who believe that they have a complaint, and particularly the young lady, Miss Moore, who was notified by the Civil Service Commission that she had received the appointment and that she should report for duty immediately.
In the British Columbian of November 3, 1928, the following letter from Miss Moore appears:
To the editor:
Perhaps you would be good enough to allow me space in your paper for the following:
A raw deal has been given to some fourteen girl stenographers and myself, all of New Westminster, by the authorities at Ottawa, or rather of New Westminster. I want to let these girls know just what has happened and how we have been so unscrupulously gulled. The examination held on August 31 for ar position in the post office was purely camouflage, which is easily seen by the way matters finished up. Three girls passed the examination, but I unfortunately, having the highest marks, was accepted by the civil service secretary and instructed to report to the postmaster immediately for duty. This was on September 28. A few days later the usual credentials as to character, health, etc., were received and duly filled in as required. (I might say that these papers were addressed to me care of the New Westminster post office.) During October I wrote the civil service secretary twice asking why the postmaster was not notified of my appointment, and may say that to date none of my letters have been answered. However, on the 29th I sent a night letter to the secretary peremptorily demanding a reply, which came on the 31st day of October informing me my services were rejected as it was a male stenographer that was required.
Now. by placing yourself in my position, you can understand what my feelings would be and how my Irish did boil. Needless to say, more anathemas than prayers were hurled at the Dominion government in Ottawa together with its satellites in New Westminster.
I would call particular attention to the following:
The only deductions one can make from the above are. that the position was never intended for any of the girl candidates; the department is guilty of extorting money from us girls without any intention of giving a quid pro quo for fees collected; there was outside interference in the course of the civil service department, or why the cancellation of the appointment?
What I would recommend is that candidates before sitting for examinations for government positions be required to show cards of approval from the party executive. That the powers that
Supply-Post Office

be make sure of the candidates' political per-suations before blocking appointments. Various other recommendations I can suggest later.
In closing I wish to strongly impress on my fellow candidates the seriousness of the situation. Our liberty is at stake as the perpetrators of an action of this kind are capable of doing anything to gain their ends, eo it is up to us to show by our resentment of such treatment that we refuse to countenance such dirty tactics in their arbitrary methods of civil service appointments. I can assure you I will leave no stone unturned to help in any way that is in my power to see that fair play is given civil service candidates.
It may be information to the "big guns" of the party in New Westminster that a promising young Liberal has been the victim of the dirtiest deal their powers could hand out.
I apologize, Mr. Editor, for taking up so much of your valuable space but would ask you to publish this in the interest of justice so that "right not might shall rule mankind and be acknowledged stronger".
Margaret I. Moore.
The suggestion which Miss Moore makes in that letter, namely, that the department never had any intention of giving this appointment to a female candidate, appears to be borne out by the statement made by the minister, because that is the reason stated why Miss Moore was not given the appointment. What is the effect of that? It is that thirteen girls were allowed to sit on this examination, and the successful candidate, who was notified that she was appointed and that She was to report for duty immediately, was no't given the place at all. Instead, the position was given temporarily to a boy of seventeen years of age on the nomination of the defeated Liberal candidate in the last election, Mr. C. C. Knight, who now resides and has been residing in the city of Ottawa for most of the time since the last election.
The file shows what happened. It seems that when a request was made for a stenographer in the New Westminster post office, there was no eligible list in the possession of the Civil Service Commission, and the commission therefore authorized the department to suggest an appointee for the position. An appointment would, of course, be only temporary, subject to confirmation, and, I presume, qualification by the person appointed. The department, having been notified to that effect, wrote to Mr. C. C. Knight, the defeated Liberal candidate, asking for his nomination. Mr. Knight nominated this boy Thomas, and at the same time stated that the boy was only seventeen years of age. When that nomination was received by the department, Mr. Knight was told that the boy could not be appointed because he was under age unless no other candidates were available. It appears that other candidates were

available because these thirteen young ladies took part in the competitive examination to which I have already referred. It was pointed out by the department that such an appointment might be made temporarily, provided that no others were available, as I stated.
This boy, Thomas, wrote on the same examination, took part in the same competition that the thirteen young ladies took part in; but he failed, he did not pass. He was, however, continued in the position. In March of this year another examination was held, and this boy, who had then reached the age of eighteen years, again took part in the competition, again failed, but is still in the position. He is still acting as stenographer in the New Westminster post office although he failed twice in examinations held by the Civil Service Commission for that particular position. I think the inference is fairly clear that he is held there by reason of the political influence which my good friend, Mr. Knight, has with the department, and that the department has been able, for the purpose of helping Mr. Knight and his friends, to keep this boy in the position notwithstanding, as I say, the fact that he is not qualified for it at all.
I find in the file a memorandum dated 6th October, 1928, from Mr. P. T. Coolican, general superintendent of postal services, in reference to this matter. I am not going to read the whole letter, but there is a side note which reads:
You need a male clerk steno. Try and keep Thomas. Write to Com.
I suppose that is the commission. That is signed "L.J.G." I suppose those are the initials of the Deputy Postmaster General. Well, they have kept Thomas in the position and he is still there. I do not know whether they are going to have another examination or not or whether they will be able to get some kind of examination that he will be able to pass. But the fact remains that during all this time Thomas is holding the position although he is not qualified to do so, first, because he was under age and second, because after he reached the age of eighteen years, he could not pass the examinations of the Civil Service Commission. It seems to me that that is a disgraceful condition of affairs. It is really a crime to allow thirteen young ladies to take part in an examination and to pay $2 each as the prescribed fee for the examination when it never was the intention of the department to have a female stenographer in the office. In any event the $2 should be refunded to each one of those young ladies.

Mr. McQUARRIE That is the unfair part of the matter. The commission notified Miss Moore, without any conditions at all, that she had been appointed to the position; that she was to report for duty immediately, and by reason of that notice from the Civil Service Commission Miss Moore resigned the position which she held, and reported for duty. The Postmaster General himself is responsible, if not his department. He says that the matter never came to his attention, but someone in the Post Office Department is surely responsible for the young lady not getting the position. I defy the Postmaster General to show from his own file that the request in this particular instance was for a male stenographer. It was nothing of the kind. No such request was made after 1925 and in this particular case it was not to fill the vacancy created by the resignation of Miss Mawson, but to fill the vacancy created by the promotion of Mr. Wade who had been appointed to the service in 1925 or 1926. has been perpetrated upon the thirteen applicants through the retention of the two-dollar-fee paid by them, that is something with which the Post Office department has absolutely nothing whatever to do. It comes entirely under the Civil Service Commission. I thinik it is not proper for the Civil Service Commission or any other branch of the government to retain the fees of unsuccessful candidates, and I think the practice should be changed. But. as I say, that is not within my province, it comes entirely under the Civil Service Commission.

If it was the intention to
employ only a male stenographer in the New Westminster office, why did not the department request that only candidates of the male persuasion be asked to write on the examination?
The Civil Service Commission again.

No, the department had
something to do with it.
I have no answer to make. It was clearly a matter of administration-not outside my province, it is true, but never submitted to me.

Mr. Coolican must have
known about it.
Certainly.

If they did not tell the
young ladies that they would be rejected on account of their sex, then the departmental officials are to blame for the injustice done.

The minister has not
yet answered my question: Whether the postmaster at New Westminster made a request that Thomas be retained in the position. If so, was that request in writing? And if in writing will he produce it?
I do not know whether the postmaster made such a request or not, but if he did so in writing I will produce the document.

If he did not do so
this statement is rather misleading. It says^-
The hon. member had better wait to see if the postmaster did so or not.

It says:
In view of the postmaster's representations, however, the services of Mr. Thomas were retained-
That can be explained in no other way than that the postmaster at New Westminster re-

quested that Thomas be retained in the position. I challenge the minister on that, and I say no such request was ever made by the postmaster. I should also like to know whether Thomas is going to be retained in the position, notwithstanding the fact that he has been unsuccessful in two examinations, which would go to prove that he is not qualified.

So long as there is no waiting list established by the Civil Service Commission as a result of examinations held under their discretion, temporary employees can be taken on at any time. The moment the commission establish such a list they forward it to the department, whereupon any temporary employee must be taken off the job and the first in order of merit on the waiting list appointed. That is the practice.
Is it the intention of the department that there shall be a male stenographer in the New Westminster office?
If the postmaster recommends it, yes.

But the postmaster
did not so recommend in this case at all, as I pointed out.
I am not prepared to admit that.

The files show there
was no recommendation on the part of the postmaster in this particular case that a male stenographer should be appointed. His request was for a stenographer, without any reference to sex. That request was made in July of last year in the letter I read.

I am not offering this as
an excuse, but simply to point out what may have happened. The information may come to the department through the inspection of the office by officials from Ottawa or from some other section of the service. They would find out the requirements of the office and report thereon when they returned to Ottawa or to their own head office. I will inquire how the request came to the department here for the employment of a male stenographer.
Then I understand the Secretary of State is going to bring down the civil service file in connection with this matter.
Yes.

To prevent any error, did
the Secretary of State make a note of the right name? I thought he wrote down Victoria.

I made the necessary

I have been looking over
the salaries of the different post offices and' am	curious to know upon	what basis	thesalaries are fixed. I will	demonstrate	mypoint by taking a few of the offices which appear below the item in the estimates with the	respective population	as given in	theCanadian Almanac of 1929. If there is a mistake in the latter figures, which I presume-are	for 1928, it must be	imputed to	the
publication. For example, the city of Medicine Hat has a population of 10,500, and the salaries paid are 855,000. The city of Fort William, which I have the honour to represent, had a population of 23,500 in 1928- it is more than that at the present time- and its salaries are $63,000. Medicine Hat,, in other words, with less than half the population gets nearly the same amount, within $16,000. And then over on the next page, take Brandon with a population of 17,000' and salaries of $71,000. Take Kingston with a population of 22,000; it has salaries of $97,000. Take New Westminster with a population of 20,500, it gets $93,000 in salaries. Moncton, with 21,000 of a population, gets-8118,000 in salaries. Saskatoon, with a population of 40.000 in 1928, gets $181,000 in salaries. And one more; Regina, with a population of 40.000, gets $331,000 in salaries. The population, it is true, jump from 10,500>
to 40,000, the highest I have named, but the salaries jump from $55,000 to $331,000, and it just strikes me that probably there is a very good explanation of it. I presume there is practically no increase over last year, but I have been a little puzzled to understand those differences. I can understand it in some cases. I purposely left out such cities as Victoria,. Vancouver, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, because while they also demonstrate the point no doubt their salaries would be greatly increased because of incoming overseas mail.
What page of the estimates are you referring to?

Pages 71 and 72. The populations, of course, are not given; I have, taken them from the Canadian Almanac for-

Supply-Post Office
1929, and I think they are correct. As I say, there is probably an. explanation for all this, but at the same time the discrepancies which exist are rather strange.

Take Moncton, for instance, with a population of about 21,000 and salaries paid $118,000, and compare it with some places that have more population and less salaries paid. Moncton's revenue previous to the establishment there of the Eaton concern was $165,000 a year. Now I think it is close to $400,000, if I am not mistaken; I am just speaking from memory. The hon. member will understand that population is not the basis of salaries at all.
Mr. MAN-ION: I quite understand that.
Mr. VE'NIOT: I -would imagine the same thing obtains in Brandon, and also in Medicine Hat, accounting for the rapid increase of revenues there. In Saskatoon and Regina, as in Moncton, the mail order houses,
I think, bring about that abnormal increase in the revenue compared with the population. And the revenue is the factor in conjunction with the volume of mail upon which salaries are based, and on which help is hired; and those salaries are established by the Civil Service Commission.

I quite understand that. Take Regina and my own city, Fort William. Fort William with a population of 23,500 has salaries of $63,000. Regina with a population of 40,000-we will take it as double- has a salary list of $321,000, or practically five times as much. I should like to know the difference in income between Fort William and Regina. Could the minister give me the incomes from those offices?

The revenue of Regina is $869,000. The Revenue of Fort William is $83,000. or nearly $800,000 more revenue at Regina. As revenue is the factor in conjunction with the volume of mail and business conditions, that can be readily understood.

Before we depart from it- perhaps this will demonstrate the minister s point, and I am not criticizing-perhaps he could give me some of the other cities that I mentioned. Take Medicine Hat, what is the revenue there? Its population is 10,o00 and its salaries are $55,000.
Medicine Hat has $39,900.
Revenue?

Just to demonstrate the point that revenue alone does not govern,
I wish to point this out: Take Medicine Hat with a population less than half that of Fort William. It has a salary list of $5o,000 against a salary list of $63,000 for Fort William, but it has a revenue of much less than half. In other words, its salary list is nearly as great as the salary list at Fort William-it is more than five-sixths-but its revenue is much less than half. Would the minister go further?
I would like to get the figures for Saskatoon.

I may say, while we are looking that up, that Medicine Hat is a large distributing point for mails, and there is a great deal more work done there than the revenue would show. That is a distributing point for different sections.
For rural mail routes and that sort of thing?
Oh, no, for railways as well; a concentration of mail there for distribution to certain points.
Would the minister give me Saskatoon on the same basis?
Saskatoon, $311,000.
Well, that 'bears the argument out better. Would the minister give me one more, Brandon?

I just wish to say that the information given me by the minister is satisfactory. 1 wished to find out what the reasons were. I presume the same conditions existed in the past, but it looked strange because I knew the populations were not so vastly different. I think the matter is reasonably well explained by the minister. At the same time I find myself wondering if the differences are all just. I am -wondering if possibly an investigation along that line might not be very worthy of consideration.
They are all lined out on a certain principle.

May I call attention now to the city of Sydney? I find that the city of Sydney has a population about the same as most of those mentioned, and its salary list is very much lower. We have Eaton's establishment there and many other concerns.

The revenue at Sydney is
about $64,000. I can assure hon. gentlemen that these salaries are all based on the work of the office and regulated by the Civil Ser-

vice Commission. Where it is necessary to increase the staff of an office the Civil Service Commission receives recommendations from the department, but those increases are never made until the commission secure all the necessary information and grant us authority. The whole thing is worked out on the basis which I tried to explain to the hon. member for Fort William a short time ago.

Yes.

I would like to
ask the Postmaster General if it is true that Mr. H. Fortier, chief inspector of service at Ottawa, is now in charge of the district superintendent's office at St. John, New Brunswick, and if so why it was found necessary to have him so placed. I would also ask why it was necessary for the chief superintendent of post office service to visit St. John on March 25 last. Yes, I shall be only too
glad to furnish the hon. gentleman with that information by bringing down all the correspondence, but I may tell him that Mr. Fortier is not now in charge of the district superintendent's office there. Mr. Fortier and Mr. Underwood were sent to St. John to study conditions in that office and district. Just here I may tell the hon. gentleman who represents St. John and others who come from the province of New Brunswick that there is some serious misunderstanding with regard to the post office administration in that city I am looking into it now in an endeavour to straighten out the matter. Mr. Fortier and Mr. Underwood, one of them an efficiency man in the matter of financial administration, so to speak, and the other an efficiency man in the matter of operation, were instructed to go and did go to St. John, where they remained for three or four days, and they have made a partial report. Their work is not finished yet, but I hope these two gentlemen may iron out certain difficulties which have arisen in that city in connection with the administration of the office and the discipline of some of the officials under the district superintendent. This is what we are now working on.	[DOT]

Who is in charge of
that office now, or who is acting as district superintendent ?
There is no acting superintendent; the regular district superintendent, Mr. H. W. Woods, is in charge.

Then who is the next
senior officer in that department.
Inspector Emerson.

In the absence of the
superintendent who takes over his duties?

There is no strict rule,

I would like to state

There is no direct rule.
What is the usual practice?

I thought I had answered

Will you allow me to answer that question?

No, not just yet. Then the minister said that there is no strict rule, that usually the senior officer takes charge, but evidently there are some exceptions. When the minister answers my question would he please tell us why Mr. Emerson did not act in the absence of the superintendent, although we understand that he was appointed to succeed him, which appointment was countermanded. In answer to the first part
of the question I have already said that there is no fixed rule. There is a practice that when the district superintendent is absent from duty but within the province or within the country, the senior officer is the man who takes his place. I might state the circumstances in connection with the case which has been referred to. The health of Mr. H. W. Woods, the district superintendent of the St. John postal district, had been failing. He had informed me of that fact himself, and I had received the information from others, and noticed it especially when I visited St. John about the end of November or early in December last. When I returned to my office I took up the question of arranging for mail transportation to the West Indies under the new steamship arrangement, to see if we could not work out some scheme to facilitate the handling of the mail. In view of the fact that Mr. Woods' health was failing, I thought that he could be placed in charge of that -work and sent to the West Indies. He could take two or three weeks to do this work and at the same time his health might be improved. Mr. Woods received instructions to that effect, and placed the senior postal inspector in charge of the work during his absence. I countermanded that order and instructed that Mr. Griffiths be placed in charge until Mr. Woods returned.
I gather that the practice of the Postmaster General is to place the next senior man in charge when the superintendent is absent from his office but still in this country.

That is not the absolute
rule.
I understood the minister to say that that was almost the invariable rule.
It is usually the practice.
But when the superintendent leaves the country the junior is put in charge. If anyone can interpret that form of reasoning I shall appreciate it very much.

I can change that around
as I think it necessary in the interest of the service. I thought it was necesary in this case, and I did so.

That is internal business which sometimes it is not well to give out, but I am prepared to assume the responsibility for my action. I felt I was justified, under the conditions existing, to do as I did.
I discovered on my initiative what was occurring.

Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) moved the second reading of Bill No. 36, to amend certain provisions of the criminal code respecting the possession of weapons.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, I explained
this bill on its inception. It has been before the house for two or three years. It was introduced by the Hon. Senator Belcourt in another place and has passed the senate, and on two or three occasions has reached the appropriate standing committee of this house. It is rather long. It involves the sale, permit for use, and having in possession of firearms. I think it is directed largely against the sale of revolvers. The hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) spoke to me about it the other day, and I understand he is quite willing that it should go to the committee so that the details of it might be examined there. If the house is of the same opinion I suggest that it should be sent on to the committee, where it can be thoroughly discussed.

This is a hardy perennial. There has been, so far as I can ascertain, no demand for

Criminal Code Amendment
legislation of this kind. We are fairly well protected in the various provinces of this Dominion by the present law. This bill, letter B of the senate, if carried out in its entirety would require that every man who had in his possession any ancient weapon as a trophy should take out an annual license for it, and the same for every such weapon in his possession, which would be absolutely foolish. And, if you run through the whole matter, the penalty is excessive. One thousand dollars and costs is the penalty for the first offence.
I do not want to take up unduly the time of the house, but the bill provides that there shall be a record kept of every sale and every transfer. In other words, if a party of hunters go out and trade rifles while on the hunt they are liable to a penalty, if this bill goes through, of $1,000 and costs. The thing is absurd on the face of it. As a matter of fact, the trouble with this country is that we are being over-legislated; we have too many laws, laws about which, in many cases, we know very little; we may be guilty of offences against those laws without any intention of doing wrong. I would therefore move, Mr. Speaker, that this bill be read a second time six months hence.

This motion is debatable, is it not? My hon. friend (Mr. Arthurs) has stated objections to the bill which I think are very sound. A great many persons carry a shot gun or a rifle into the woods on perfectly legitimate business, or for the sake of sport, and they do not want to be embarrassed. But that can be attended to very well in committee. There are one or two other features in this bill, however, that should not be lost sight of. One is the procuring of revolvers by the criminal class. This bill has been endorsed by the police constables' association. I notice a letter here from the chiefs of police of Toronto and Montreal. Toronto and Montreal are centres in which great difficulty has been experienced of late in dealing with criminals, all of whom, apparently, carry firearms. The chiefs of police are officials who have in their hands the ferreting out and prosecuting of criminals, and they think that if there was some way of tracing the weapon with which they are armed when caught it might be of great use.
I am sorry to say that I cannot add much more than that. My friend says there is no demand for such legislation. There certainly is a demand from the police department. If there are details in the bill which have to do, in some wa3% with the disposal by a shopkeeper of his stock in trade, or a sportsman having in his possession a rifle or a shot gun, 
I think the committee can very well take care of that. The main purpose of the bill, as I see it, is to restrict the holding of revolvers and arms of that type by people unauthorized to hold them, and to restrict in such a way the purchase of revolvers that they will not get into the hands of people who should not be entrusted with them. That is the principle of the bill. One might speak for an hour on it and get no further than that. I suggest that as the house has had the courtesy to send this to the appropriate committee in other years, where it has rested, unable to get further because of prorogation following soon after, we might do the same with it this year and there defeat it, if we please.

Why waste the time?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): I gathered from my hon. friend (Mr. Geary) that he had di&-cussed this matter with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and that the minister had no objection to the bill going to committee in order that it might be further examined.
That was it; he expressly stated so.

I have on numerous occasions in this house voted against killing a bill without adequate discussion, and for the principle of referring bills of this character to committees in order that they might be further inquired into, even though I might oppose the bill itself. For that reason I feel inclined to vote against the six month's hoist before adequate discussion of the measure has taken place. I think it should be discussed and examined before the appropriate committee. That is only fair, and, for that reason, speaking for myself only, of course,
I shall vote against this form of closure.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
This bill has been before the house on previous occasions and has been discussed at very great length. The objections, which have been pointed out and which I think are valid, are numerous indeed. One reason why I think this bill should be defeated on its second reading is that its promoters, who, from our previous discussions, can learn something of the sentiment of the house, should take a reasonable time to redraft the ' bill and bring it before the house in more simplified form so that it may be expected to accomplish the objects which they state they have in view, and eliminate those parts of the bill which seem to be utterly ludicrous.

Criminal Code Amendment
1S59

Two years ago, if I remember rightly, Mr. Speaker, I was sponsor for the bill introduced at that time in the senate by Senator Belcourt. Numerous objections to the proposed legislation were raised in the house; the bill was referred to a committee and, if my memory is correct, most of the objections to the bill were overcome by changes which were made in that committee and the bill in its new form was far more acceptable than when it was first presented. I feel very much like my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning); instead of killing this bill outright by supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) I would suggest that it be referred to a committee where the interested parties might appear.
Has my hon. friend read the bill?

I have read the bill. I would not say that I approve of all its provisions but I think it might be sent to a committee before which the interested people could appear, instead of killing it as we will if we support the amendment.

I think this bill has been before this house five times. On one occasion it was sent to a committee which amended it very considerably, but now it is brought back to the house almost in its original form. I do not see any object in taking up the time of parliament by appointing a special committee; so mans' committees are meeting now that no one would have time to attend the meetings of such a committee. Let the promoters of this bill revise it and bring it back in a more acceptable form. It has waited five years now, and no injury has been done.

I think the point of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) is well taken, and as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has indicated, this bill has been discussed on several previous occasions. I remember once when it was absolutely laughed out of the house because it was so ridiculous, so it is hardly an argument for members of the government to suggest that this amendment is a form of closure in connection with this bill.

subsubtopic: EIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
I think at the outset, Mr. Speaker,, it would be well if I read the bill, since there appears to be a feeling on the part of some members of the house that the bill has something to do with the divorce laws of Canada. That is not the case; it has no bearing at all upon the laws now governing divorce in this country except that it will enable the women of Canada to enter actions for divorce upofi the same grounds as those upon which they are now instituted by the men. The bill provides as follows:
1.	This act may be cited as The Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1929.
2.	For the purposes of this act a married woman,
(a)	who is judicially or otherwise separate and living separate and apart from her husband; or
(b)	who either before or after the passing of this act has been deserted by and lived separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years, and is still living apart from her husband;
may acquire a domicile for herself as though she were a feme sole and may commence an action for divorce praying that her marriage may be dissolved on any grounds that entitle her to such divorce in any court having jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii.

The bill, I repeat, has no bearing whatever upon the present divorce laws of Canada. I make that explanation in order to clear the minds of those who think that we are attempting to make divorce easier, or anything of that kind.
It is, I understand, the settled law that in Canada the domicile of a married woman is the domicile of her husband no matter where he happens to be. It is also I understand, the law that the jurisdiction of the provincial courts in provinces where there is provision for divorce, and the jurisdiction of parliament, depend on the question whether the applicant is domiciled, in the one case in the province, and in the other in the Dominion of Canada.
There are many women in Canada whose husbands have deserted them and in some cases remarried and settled in other countries -in this case another province is another dominion or another country-and these women are deprived of the right of obtaining a divorce by reason of this rule of law. I know of three or four such cases in my own riding, and, considering the position which has been given to woman with respect to property, the exercise of the franchise and many other matters, I think it is time that she was put on the same .basis as her husband with reference to his important domestic matter. In other words, I believe that the old rule of law making the woman's domicile absolutely dependent upon the domicile of her husband should be altered and that woman should be given the right to establish a domicile of her own, separate and independent from that of the husband. This is only a matter of common sense, reason and fair play. There is no sound reason why an obsolete rule of law should be invoked to deprive women throughout Canada of access to the courts in order to obtain redress in the same way that men can. I am urging it for the consideration of the house simply for this reason.
In my own province and the neighbouring provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and BriV'sh Columbia the courts have jurisdiction in divorce. Any man, no matter where his wife lives, can come to any of these four provinces, acquire a domicile and seek redress from the courts by way of divorce. But women who have lived all their lives in these provinces, who are citizens and voters and in many cases large property owners paying taxes and generally carrying out all the honourable demands of society, are denied the right of access to the courts because it happens that their husbands have deserted them and acquired a domicile in some foreign country. It is ridiculous to say that because the woman's husband has deserted her and has gone to

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
Mexico, Australia or China, her domicile is removed to one of those places. I know women who have never left the province of Manitoba but who have been told that their domicile is in England, South Africa or the United States. For these reasons I have thought fit to bring in this bill and urge it upon the attention of the house.
As I know that this matter involves a great many difficult questions of law and as I am a layman, I am presenting it to the house for consideration in this general way in the hope that a number of the lawyers in the house will join in the debate and express their views on the subject. I know that many hon. members of the legal profession are familiar with the question and can give us a full explanation of the points involved, considered from the standpoint of the law.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was very sorry indeed to hear the words of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) a few moments ago, because he touched only one remote phase of the question. I would like to submit to the house one type case in which gross injustice is now being done. Take the case of a married couple residing in any given place: the husband deserts his wife-and it is not an unusual thing -he goes away and the wife remains in her home town or locality. That is not her domicile, because her husband has run away and grossly deserted her. She is the victim of his evil propensities. That is undoubtedly an injustice to the decent womanhood which finds itself in that position. I have, for instance, knowdedge of a case in a western city where a young couple, both minors, were married. Their parents found the youngsters and they were separated. The young man went away and the woman, who was under age and who was married to him, is living still, as she was then, in the home of her parents. Ten years have passed. They do not know where the young man has gone. He has vanished, and she has no domicile except her husband's unknown domicile, wherever that may be. In regard to what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has just said about the question of property and many other rights, they are determined upon the ipse dixit of this chap who has run away.

My hon. friend will remember that I prefaced my remarks by saying that this was just my personal opinion; that I was not speaking for the government.

But the Solicitor General is speaking as solicitor general of a government and weight is attached to his words not only because of his position, but also because of his great legal learning in regard to these matters.

There is one observation which I should like to add to the remarks that have been made. It seems to me that there is also in this bill a principle of wide concern and application to the people of Canada, that is, the matter of equal rights of the womanhood of this country in comparison with the rights the men hold. There has been through modem times a strong development in equalizing the social, political and economic rights of the womanhood of this country. This is not a question of the principle of divorce; it is not a question where the convictions of any hon. member should interfere with his sense of justice and duty to the womanhood of Canada with regard to its right to equal treatment with the men of Canada. I am one of those who believe that the time has arrived in our civilization when the women of Canada, and, in fact, of ether countries, do not have to regard

themselves as having an inferiority complex, or rather, when the men should not regard themselves as possessing a superiority complex. I should like to place before the house the simple thought that underlying this bill is the fact that the attitude of the house will be a declaration whether or not the parliament of Canada, which unfortunately possesses only one woman and a good one at that, will deny to the women the principle of equal treatment in this matter as well as in all social, political and economic matters.
