Postmaster General will get far more credit for action this session than he will if he delays until next year; it will be more genuine if it comes during this session than if he waits until the eve of a general election. Why can we not get some support for this application from Liberal members opposite? Why can not we get some backing from the Liberal Progressives in this house Why have they remained silent during five days of this discussion?
They have not had a chance to speak.

They will have a chance in a few moments. I believe that if any considerable number will back my proposal we will succeed this session in righting this wrong, because it is a wrong.
This government cannot say that they cannot afford it; after the 'budget speech we know they can afford it. The 2,700 letter carriers in Canada could each be paid $200 a year more for the amount of money spent last year on motor cars, according to the Auditor General's report; you could pay them $200 a year each for the $500,000 you wasted for a house in Washington; you could pay them another large amount for the tens of thousands of dollars you have been wasting in North Bruce in order to elect a minister of the crown at the next general election. A minister of finance who comes to parliament and closes his financial year on April 1 with a surplus of $60,000,000 in his treasury can pay every one of these 10,000 postal workers an additional $250 this year; that will take $2,500,000 of his surplus and still leave him $57,500,000 to play around with. Do not say the country cannot afford it this year. This is the year to make the application, the year in which we have the surplus that has been referred to, while men are receiving from this government a rate of pay which will not enable them to maintain their families in decency.
Surely this is a situation which must be remedied.. Year after year the request is made; year after year I fancy ministers are deluged with requests, of which I suppose every member of the house receives copies. But whether the government are too careless about it, whether they are too much occupied with other matters, whether the time of the Postmaster General is too much occupied in. dismissing postmasters and hunting up new men for these offices, I know not. I feel like advising the postal workers to take what satisfaction they may out of that parable of our Lord in respect to the unjust judge..
Supply-Post Office

I do not suppose in this committee anyone but myself and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will recognize the reference, but if the postal workers will look up the eighteenth chaper of St. Luke they will find that in a certain city there was a judge who feared not God nor regarded man. There was also a widow in that city who came unto him asking him to avenge her of her enemy and he would not for a while, but afterwards said. "Though I fear not God, nor regard man, yet because this widow troUbleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me." Now I think we had better tell the underpaid officials in 'the Post Office department to keep up their requests until they .succeed in wearying the Postmaster General and worrying this government, and on the principle expounded in the parable of the unjust judge perhaps some day they may succeed. However, I can assure them that in any event they have not very long to wait; soon there will be in power in this country a government which will listen to their appeals and which will be prepared to satisfy promptly every just and reasonable demand.
I hope I have not said anything harsh to the Postmaster General; I realize that he received a very doubtful compliment this afternoon when he obtained a majority of only twenty-seven on the vote on the amendement and his feelings at the moment may be a little ruffled. I am trying to appeal to his sense of justice and of fair play. Here is the opportunity ; here is the grievance; here is the government with a surplus of $60,000,000, a government which at times can be wildly extravagant. Surely we can get a little additional salary for the letter carriers, the postal workers, the postal porters and all the others included in those 10,005 men now working day in and day out for the Post Office department, a great many of whom are not being paid enough money to keep body and soul together.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised to find that my hon. friend has been driven to such an extremity that he quotes sacred history in order to -plead the case of the postal workers, or perhaps I should say he w-as appealing to the galleries in order to cover up the inconsistencies of which he and his -party were guilty when the postal workers appealed to them when they were in power in 1919 and again in 1921. At that time they asked for bread and were given a stone.
They were given more than they are getting now. They were given a bonus then, w-hi'ch they are not getting now.

When the postal workers of the country appealed to the government of that day they were referred to the Griffenhagen commission, and through that commission they were -placed under the Civil Service Commission as it is now constituted. From that day to this they have been under that commission; that was the response given by the Tory party to the appeals made by the postal workers of that day.
We gave -them the bonus.

There has been no necessity for the postal workers of Canada to be afraid to appeal to the Liberal government on any occasion, at least since I have had the honour of being Postmaster General. The postal workers will testify that on all occasions, at all times and in every possible way they have received my sympathetic su-pport and that on different occasions I have strongly recommended to the Civil Service Commission that they consider the situation of the poorly paid postal workers of Canada. I guaranteed to the Civil Service Commission that the government was, -prepared to place in the estimates an -amount sufficient -to cover the higher classification and the increased wages they might recommend for the postal workers, the postal clerks, the postal helpers and the railway mail clerks of Canada. I have failed in my efforts as far as the -postal helpers, postal workers -and postal clerks are concerned. I have partly-succeeded with regard to the railway mail clerks, and in the estimates this year there is an a-mount to cover increases in salary to -the railway mail clerks as recommended by the Civil Service Commission.
My hon. friend says there is an easy way of accomplishing this end; -according to him all we have to do is place in the supplementary estimates an amount of money sufficient to -meet the increases -to which we consider these postal workers entitled. Why, Mr. Chairman, last night I was roundly denounced by the hon. gentleman's leader 'because I was not living up to the spirit a-nd the letter of the Civil Service Act.
I grant that, but-

I did not interrupt my hon. friend when he was speaking. To-night I am asked by the first lieutenant of the leader of the opposition to ignore completely the Civil Service Act and place this amount in the supplementary estimates, while as an old parliamentarian my hon. friend knows that cannot 'be done without an amendment to the Civil Service Act as it stands to-day.

Is parliament supreme?

Supply-Post Office

If a supplementary estimate is brought down and voted by parliament contrary to the statute, the Auditor General would refuse to recognize it. Everyone knows that he is supreme in these matters, and no one knows it better than the hon. gentleman who is now leading the opposition in the absence of his leader. They talk about the poor postal helpers, the small pay they are receiving, and such things, but talking to the galleries in this house is quite cheap.
Who is looking for the spotlight now?

I would like to give the house once more the evidence of what this government has attempted to do to encourage the Civil Service Commission in recognizing the just claims of those who are classified as postal workers, postal helpers and postal clerks. I would like to read the last communication I sent to the Civil Service Commission after they had refused point blank to consider the recommendation made by myself that an increase be made in the salaries of these men. This matter had been under consideration for nearly one year and I had written to them pointing out that the estimates had to be arranged for the coming year and that it was the intention to place sufficient in the general estimates to meet an increase in salary to the postal helpers, postal workers and postal clerks, provided the commission would do its duty and recommend such an increase. They replied on March 9, refusing to comply with my request, and on March 11 I wrote as follows:
I note you say that the matter has been placed before the board of commissioners and that after full consideration of the subject matter contained in my letter the commissioners have decided to confirm their decision of May 2. 1928. which was that further increase in the compensation of these classes is not justified.
That is the decision of the very body which the hon. members contended last night I should follow in every respect. That is their answer, and they are the only ones qualified to give an answer. The letter continued:
I wish to thank you for the information but at the same time I regret that your commission has not seen fit to accept the recommendation of the department in favour of the postal clerks, letter carriers and mail porters, because I am convinced that they are deserving of better pay than they are now receiving.
That is the policy laid down by myself with the full authority of the government. When that was placed before the Civil Service Commission they refused absolutely to take advantage of the power given them un-78594-119
der the statute to grant an increase, and they say the increase is not justified. The hon. gentleman may appeal to every kind of feeling and prejudice, but the fact remains that that commission, placed there by them when the postal workers were appealing for a living wage, and when they were in a position to grant it without any reference to the commission, refused to grant such an increase. Hon. members may pound their desks-we know exactly what that means-but the fact still remains that when the hon. members opposite had the power to increase the salaries of these men they ignored that opportunity and placed the power in the hands of the very commission which is saying today that they are not justified in accepting a recommendation that these poorly paid employees of the government should receive an increase in salary.

Mr. Chairman, I am inclined to think that the Postmaster General misconceives the actual situation. He says that we on this side of the house expect him to live up to the letter and the spirit of the Civil Service Act-we certainly do, and in every particular. We expect the government to do the same thing. But how can it be said that parliament is bound by its own creature? Is this Civil Service Cimmission an autocracy? Are they above the will of the people as expressed in parliament? It is nonsense to say that they are.
Change the act.

The power that created
it can change or destroy it. I do not advocate its destruction, but I say that the minister is not blocked, nor is this government blocked if it desires to bring in an estimate containing the words "notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act." That action would be perfectly valid; it is constitutional it is the will of parliament which is supreme. The minister is not supreme; he is bound by not only the letter but the spirit of the act. So is this government 'bound by the act, and we expect them to live up to it. I am pointing out to them a way out of the difficulty. The minister says that he realizes that these men are underpaid. He says, "I have made a plea to the commission and the commission will not grant it; I know their case is a just one, but the commission will not consider it." The position has only to be stated to reveal its absurdity. My complaint is that the Postmaster General has not shown any willingness to grant these men a living wage. A government which can



Supply-Post Office

squander millions of dollars and still have $60,000,000 of a surplus in the treasury, surely can find a way to pay a living wage to men who, as everybody in Canada knows, are not receiving such a wage.

To prove to the house that the hon. gentleman is not interpreting the opinion of the postal workers, in a part of Canada at least, I would like to read to the house a telegram which I received this morning. This telegram is dated at Toronto, which is not exactly a Liberal stronghold, and is addressed to the Postmaster General at Ottawa. It reads:
We, the postal workers of the department in Toronto, desire to go on record as strongly opposing the tactics being used to discredit you and your efforts in promoting the improvement you have and are inaugurating in the service.
That is sent on behalf of some three or four thousand postal workers in the city of Toronto. The telegram is signed by E. J. Purvis.
Who is he?

He is one of the head
executives.

I have received letters from
the city of Toronto within the past few days which ask for the very things which have been recommended by the hon. member for South Wellington. I have one letter signed by A. MeMordie, the national president of the organization.

I have received letters
also.

I would like to deal for a
moment with the remarks of the Postmaster General. It seems to me an extraordinary position that we find ourselves in at the present time. We have the Liberal party, through the Postmaster General, saying that they are in favour of giving to the postal employees an increase in their pay; we have the Conservative party also committeed to the same principle, and I am sure I can speak for all those who sat in this corner of the house that we are also in favour of giving to the postal workers an increase in their present remuneration. Therefore the house is practically unanimous on a certain course of action, and there are three individuals who stand in the way of that action being consummated. If the government were anxious to put into operation the increase in the salaries of the postal workers, I believe, they could very easily find ways and means of doing so.
We will do it if you give us a chance.

Yes. When the Postmaster General spoke a few moments ago he said, I think, that he had advised his colleagues in the cabinet that he was prepared that they should grant an increase to the postal employees. I hope I am not doing an injustice to him, because I could not hear very well what he had to say. I jotted it down as he spoke, and I understood him to say that he could not convince his colleagues in the cabinet.

I did not. I would not
say that.

I said: I hope I am not
doing him an injustice. I understood him to say that he could not convince his colleagues to insert in the estimates an item for an increase in salary to the postal employees.
No. Take it back .

If he did not say that, I
absolutely withdraw that statement. I could not hear him very well. Did he convince his colleagues to that effect?

If the hon. member will
allow me, I said that in communicating with the commission and asking them to grant the increases we recommended, I wanted it done because it was the intention to place the item in the estimates for this year. I was doing it with i,he consent of the government, and therefore I was laying down the government policy.

What is there at the present juncture to prevent the placing in the estimates of an amount that will take care of the increases to the postal workers? I understand the question was raised that the Auditor General might object to such an item being placed in the estimates. I think the government can do in that respect exactly as they have done in many others. If there is any doubt on the question, they can say something like this: "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act," this item goes into the estimates. Then we overcome the difficulty so far as the Civil Service Act is concerned. For instance, the Washington item for $100,000 in the estimates reads:
Representation, including salaries and allowances for minister plenipotentiary, secretaries and staff, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act, or any of its amendments.

Supply-Procedure
If this appears so many times in the estimates for 1930, there is no reason why the same thing should not apply in regard to the postal workers.
Let me go a little further. The Postmaster General referred to the question of observing the letter of the act, stating that by not granting to the postal employees the increase proposed, he was not overruling the Civil Service Commission. He knows as well as I do, and as well as any other hon. member does, that within the past few days the government have overridden a decision of the Civil Service Commission in regard to salaries. I am referring to the question of the salaries of the technical employees. The Civil Service Commission made a recommendation to the government. It makes no difference whether they recommended an increase or anything else; the fact is they made a recommendation to the government, but the government refused to accept it. The government have also refused to accept the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission in connection with the salaries of the postal employees. Why should there be a difference between the higher paid men and the lower paid men of the service to the disadvantage of the latter? If the government were to show any consideration in this particular question, it should be to the lower paid men in its service. They have appointed a commission. This commission was constituted by order in council, so that the whole government were responsible for its appointment. The other day I asked the Postmaster General to do exactly with the loiter paid postal employees as the government did with the technical employees who may be receiving anything up to $7,000 or $8,000 a year. The postal employees have appealed to the minister; they have appealed to the Civil Service Commission; they have appealed to parliament, and they have been turned down in every case. What are they to do? If they went on strike, we would hear a howl from one end of the country to the other. What does the Postmaster General expect these low paid postal workers to do at the present juncture in order to obtain redress? If he can answer that question, I shall be satisfied.
I cannot answer that question.

I want that question
answered, and yet the minister sits in his place and says that he is unable to answer it. I know it is a difficult question; but will he answer this one:	How does he expect
a government employee and his family to live on $85 a month? I know he cannot answer 78594-119.$
that question. We as members of the house have some responsibility in this matter because they are employees of the government, and as was pointed out by the hon. member for South Toronto, we ought at least to be model employers in regard to those who work for the government. I do not think there is in the house anyone who will say that $85 or $100 a month is anything like an adequate living wage.
Let me come to other cases where the government are able to grant increases. In regard to the deputy ministers they grant them increases amounting to $1,000 and $2,000 per annum and the question of the Civil Service Commission does not enter into the matter at all; but when the question is one of the lower paid employees, there always seems to be an obstacle in the way of giving them that to which I believe they are absolutely entitled.
Progress reported.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROCEDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
SUPPLY-PROCEDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
By leave of the house,
may I be allowed to give the ruling I promised
yesterday?
On Wednesday, April 17, Mr. Robb moved that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply.
Mr. Stewart (Leeds) moved in amendment that all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this house, the Postmaster General has acted in a most arbitrary manner and in utter disregard of the letter and the spirit of the Civil Service Act in connection with the recent appointment of a postmaster at the town of Simcoe.
Debate thereon was interrupted on Wednesday at six o'clock by the adjournment of the house under standing order 6; and on Thursday, the 18th, when the order was called for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply, I had to leave the chair without question put, under standing order 28. This rule which does away with a motion for the house to go in supply on Thursday and Friday was passed in 1913. The revision of 1927 did not deal with this matter.
The leader of the house- having agreed that debate continue on Mr. Stewart's amendment, there was no necessity to give a ruling, but the house requested that I render a decision in order to settle the practice which should be followed in the future under the same circumstances.
1S80
Supply-Procedure

I have listened with great interest to the able argument set forth by several prominent members and I have carefully compared our standing orders with those of Great Britain. Standing orders 6, 7 and 28 must be construed together in accordance with the broad statement laid down by Lord Mansfield, namely:
Where there are different statutes in pari materia, though made at different times, or even expired and not referring to each other, they shall be taken and construed together, as one system and as explanatory of each other.
I have come to the conclusion that if debate on the amendment to the motion for leaving the chair is interrupted by the eleven o'clock adjournment, as was the case last year, the procedure is not annihilated but suspended by the operation of standing order 28, because standing order 7 provides that:
All business not disposed of at the termination of the sitting shall stand over until the next sitting day when it will be taken up at the same stage where its progress was interrupted.
It is well established under our practice that the expression "next sitting," "next sitting day" and "next sitting of the house" when used to state the time until which a question is ordered to stand over do not mean the following calendar day, but rather the next day on which it will be convenient to resume the proceedings on that question. It seems, therefore, that if debate is interrupted at eleven o'clock under standing order 7, the question is not superseded or lapsed, but it can be resumed without a motion to that effect on the first occasion that motion is made for the Speaker to leave the chair for supply, which may be on any of the three first sitting days of the following week. Sir Erskine May's comments on this point do not entirely apply to our House of Commons because the eleven o'clock rule at Westminster is not the same as ours. I am of the opinion that no motion is necessary for the resumption of this debate when it is interrupted at eleven o'clock.
But the situation is different if the interruption is caused by adjournment of the debate at any time or by the adjournment of the house at six o'clock on Wednesday. Standing order 27 provides that the question then under consideration shall stand in a certain precedence on the order paper, but no order is therein given to proceed with it. In that case, I am of the opinion that May's comments, as found at page 527 of the 13th

edition, will apply. The procedure on the amendment lapses. But can it be revived?
The answer must be given from the broadest point of view possible. It must not be forgotten that when the house passed standing order 7 compelling adjournment at eleven o'clock, it very materially curtailed the length of debate in such cases as the one under consideration.
Formerly an amendment involving want of confidence could be discussed from Monday until Wednesday at six o'clock in the afternoon without interruption and the question could be exhausted in that time, but now with only six hours' sittings on Monday and Tuesday and three hours on Wednesday, it seems that the minority or, as it is called, the opposition, is at a great disadvantage, as Thursday may be reached before all the members who wish to speak have had an opportunity to do so.
If the question lapses, an expression of opinion cannot be given by the house on what may be a most important grievance. The government's policy can neither be vindicated nor challenged. I do not think such a situation was ever contemplated by the authors of standing order 28 or by the committee which recommended standing order 7 in 1927. It is a well-known principle in parliamentary law that the House of Commons can rescind its own decisions, suspend its own orders or revive any superseded motion.
No notice is necessary in Great Britain for a motion to revive an order of the day which has been dropped or set aside by abrupt adjournments or any other procedure. But our standing order 45 leaves no room for doubt. Every resolution of the house, and that means every decision, must be preceded by a notice.
I think I am on safe ground in ruling that when an amendment like Mr. Stewart's is removed from the order paper by the operation of standing order 28, the question itself does not lapse, but the procedure thereon is suspended over Thursday and Friday, and a motion to resume (I say advisedly "resume" and not revive) may be made after notice, but this resumption must take place the first time that the ministry moves the house into supply, and by neglecting to do so on that occasion, the mover waives his right to bring up his amendment at a later date.
In giving a decision which will settle our parliamentary jurisprudence for the future, I must not lose sight of the principle that the

Questions
right of the commons to challenge the administration of public affairs should be fully preserved.
This house,
as Lord Palmerston said,
is the mouthpiece of the nation, the organ by which all opinions, all complaints, all notices of grievances, all hopes and expectations, all wishes and suggestions which may arise among the people at large, may be brought to an expression, may be discussed, examined, answered, rejected or redressed.
In the present case, Mr. Stewart (Leeds) should have moved after due notice that the debate be resumed on his amendment as soon as the government made the motion that I leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply.
Last year, debate could have been resumed automatically and without a special motion on Doctor Tolmie's amendment which had been interrupted at eleven o'clock by the operation of standing order 7.
Two different situations arise in the premises because the application of standing order 28 depends upon the interpretation of standing orders 7 and 27.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, April 24, 1929
